articles.title: NFL Power Rankings entering Week 8: Vikings are last undefeated team, but are they No. 1?
articles.summary: Minnesota has a championship level defense and Seattle is the only other team with a decent argument for a better group. But the Vikings don't have the balan...
articles.body:
NFC East: Cowboys | Giants | Eagles | Commanders NFC North : Bears | Lions | Packers | Vikings NFC South: Falcons | Panthers | Saints | Buccaneers NFC West: Cardinals | Rams | 49ers | Seahawks

AFC East: Bills | Dolphins | Patriots | Jets AFC North: Ravens | Bengals | Browns | Steelers AFC South: Texans | Colts | Jaguars | Titans AFC West: Broncos | Chiefs | Raiders | Chargers

One of the themes to this NFL season is a lack of permanence.

Every time a team starts to look good, they take a bad loss. Teams we thought would be fantastic this season are hanging around .500 or below it. The circle of trust is small through seven weeks. In that scope, what the Minnesota Vikings have done is impressive.

It's not even Halloween and there's just one team left without a loss. That's the Vikings, who had the longest odds to win the NFC North coming into the season. Simply winning every game in this chaotic season is worth praise. It's not like anyone else could do it.

Does that make the Vikings the best team in the NFL? That's way more complicated. Oddsmakers aren't convinced. Minnesota is tied for 10th in Super Bowl odds at BetMGM. DVOA isn't convinced. The Vikings are ranked sixth there. Part of that is the Vikings have played the third-easiest schedule in the NFL, according to DVOA. Their future schedule is the fifth-toughest.

The reason for any skepticism is obvious: The Vikings' offense isn't very good. Minnesota is 29th in EPA (expected points added) per play, 30th in offensive DVOA, 29th in yards gained and 29th in passing yards. Against a bad Colts defense Sunday, the Vikings' offense was as healthy as it has been all season. The Vikings had six points through three quarters until they rallied for 10 points in the fourth quarter to win. The Vikings have failed to surpass 275 yards in four of six games. They've scored more than 23 points only once this season. Kyler Murray was a bargain addition at quarterback this offseason after the lowly Cardinals cut him, and the Vikings are getting what they're paying for.

Minnesota has a championship level defense and Seattle is the only other team with a decent argument for a better group. But the Vikings don't have the balance of other elite NFL teams. The 49ers were clearly the most impressive team in the NFL coming into Week 7, and the only difference in Week 7 was that San Francisco had a bunch of injuries for a tricky early start at Atlanta and lost , while the Vikings had an easy matchup against the Colts at home and barely won. Those results don't make the Vikings suddenly better than the 49ers, or the best team in the league. They aren't yet. It just means Minnesota is the last undefeated team.

There's still time for the Vikings to prove without a question they are the best team in the NFL, with a stellar defense and perhaps an offense that will improve. But they're not there yet. However, they are the only team without a loss, and that's all that will really matter in Minnesota for now.

Here are the NFL power rankings after Week 7 of the NFL season:

The Chargers are the last winless team in the NFL, which nobody saw coming two months ago. And it might be a while until they get their first win. The next three games come against the Rams, Texans and Ravens. Then on Nov. 22 the Chargers host the Jets, so they'll have a shot at a win then if they don't pull an upset in their next three games.

Everyone will be watching to see if coordinator Mike McDaniel can turn around the offense. There was speculation the Chargers might remove him from that role over the bye week, but they didn't. Everyone in the offense is underachieving. And now the Chargers have three tough matchups in a row.

The Titans are not a good team, but the hope lies in them turning around their luck in close games. Three times in the final minute they've had a chance to win, but against the Eagles and Browns they gave up drives to lose in the final seconds, and against the Giants they threw an interception into the end zone. Tennessee isn't good enough to finish those games, but at least there's some reason to believe they're not as far off as their record indicates.

Titans head coach Robert Saleh went out of his way to defend Cam Ward after the last-second loss to the Browns. Ward had 181 yards and an interception for a 66.7 passer rating.

"You can't possibly watch that film and say Cam Ward did not play good, winning football. You can't," Saleh said, via the team's site. "Now there's things you have to fix, but if anyone is trying to pin this loss on him you are just trying to make s*** up."

It's just a matter of time for Aaron Glenn. He's 5-19 and Sunday brought a new low, losing to a previously winless Dolphins team that the Jets clearly have a talent edge against. The Jets never led in the game. It wouldn't have surprised anyone if Glenn was the first coach fired this season on Monday, though the Jets made no such decision.

One unbelievable stat got attention Sunday: New York has been outscored 107-6 in the final two minutes of the first half through Glenn's 24 games. On Sunday, Glenn made the curious decision to not call timeouts late in the first half with the Dolphins in the red zone, which could have preserved time for the offense to answer. Glenn said he thought his defense would get a stop, but "maybe we should have" used the timeouts. Either way, the continued failures late in the half are startling.

"If I were them, I would do two-minute every day of my life until further notice," former Steelers head coach Mike Tomlin said on NBC .

The Dolphins can relax. There was always the hope that the team with the NFL's thinnest roster could beat the Jets in one of their two meetings, and that happened. Everyone focuses on the winless teams in the NFL but nobody remembers the one-loss teams, so the Dolphins are spared a lot of grief that would have come had their winless season continued through November. They're still probably not the 29th best team in the NFL but they deserved a bump up after outplaying the Jets.

"It was a really, really special moment, one that I'm appreciative of and one that I won't forget. It was fun," Dolphins head coach Jeff Hafley said, according to Associated Press. "They deserve it. You could feel a lot come out of it. I'm very happy for the players. They did a great job."

For a while, it looked like the Colts might beat the NFL's only remaining undefeated team. Indianapolis led 10-6 at halftime and that lead held through the third quarter. But in the fourth quarter the Colts were outscored 10-0 and it was just another loss for a team that has already fired its general manager and has to be considering a change at head coach too.

Coach Shane Steichen is being asked if he'll consider a quarterback change. Steichen said he hasn't considered replacing Daniel Jones with Anthony Richardson Sr. Jones' passer rating is down to 69.4. Richardson hasn't been good in the NFL but at some point something has to change. Steichen may not consider it, but he might not be the one making that call by the end of the season.

There's so much going wrong with the Cardinals that it's not like a quarterback change would make a difference. Jacoby Brissett isn't the reason Arizona is losing, and rookie Carson Beck isn't going to fix much. But there's not much else to discuss around that team so head coach Mike LaFleur will be asked about it after every loss. After losing to the Broncos on Sunday, LaFleur again confirmed that Brissett is his QB1.

The Cardinals are wasting another great season by tight end Trey McBride, who had 10 catches for 111 yards Sunday. McBride leads the NFL with 59 receptions and has 472 yards. He is on an early Hall of Fame pace, and the Cardinals are 21-52 in games he has played.

It could get ugly in Philadelphia the rest of the season. This was a team that started the season with legitimate hope of being a Super Bowl contender. They could end up with a top-five draft pick in April.

There is still enough talent on the roster to be competitive in games, but the effort in the second half against Dallas wasn't inspiring . The offense quit moving the ball and the defense really let down. The Cowboys, who had been struggling to run the ball, had 204 yards on the ground. Dak Prescott threw three touchdown passes. The Eagles were completely flat on defense for most of Monday night.

Young teams can sometimes play well in the second half of the season as they keep fighting, like the Saints did last season. That usually doesn't happen for teams that have recently won a championship, were expected to compete for another this season and are already out of the race before the end of October.

It seems more and more like the Saints just caught an easy part of their schedule late last season, throwing everyone off on how good they could be. In a loss to the Steelers, the Saints' running backs had 11 yards on 14 carries. The defense got only two stops the entire game. A missed field goal in the fourth quarter was a big blow. The Saints simply aren't a very good team.

Everything going forward is framed through an ominous message last week from Saints owner Gayle Benson, who was clearly not happy with the team's start this season.

"[Head coach] Kellen Moore and his coaches are responsible for preparing our players to perform," Benson said at a gathering of the Greater New Orleans Quarterback Club, according to the Associated Press . "[General manager] Mickey Loomis and our football staff are responsible for building a roster capable of sustained success. The players are responsible for their preparation and execution. I am responsible for holding this organization accountable.

"Words will not restore our fans' confidence. Our performance must do that."

24. Washington Commanders (1-4-1, LW: 25)

The big question for the Commanders coming out of the bye will be how to replace top receiver Terry McLaurin, who is done for the season with a torn patellar tendon. Stefon Diggs' role will increase, though he is miscast as a top option at this point in his career. Tight end Chig Okonkwo had season highs with seven catches on seven targets last week, and his usage will have to increase without McLaurin. Rookie receiver Antonio Williams, a third-round draft pick who has shown flashes, has a big opportunity ahead.

The Commanders are 1-4-1 but not completely out of the NFC East race due to the malaise elsewhere in the division. But the Commanders first need to figure out how to adequately replace their best pass catcher.

Nobody counted on the Buccaneers scoring 43 points with Baker Mayfield having just 64 passing yards. The Panthers were very sloppy on Sunday, but the Buccaneers had something to do with that. The 43-13 win gave new life to Tampa Bay's season.

Tampa Bay, which was 1-5 before Sunday, now has a 32.5% chance to win the NFC South, according to DVOA . That's the second-best chance, and not far behind Carolina at 36.3%. Now, with Mayfield healthy — presumably anyway, it was hard to tell in 11 low-stress passing attempts in his return from a dislocated thumb — and in a bad division, the Buccaneers can feel like their season is alive even with just two wins.

"You don't change the process just because of the results," Mayfield said, according to the team's site . "We've been working on how to play together, how to come together, so to see it come together in a win like this, guys can continue to build on that."

The Raiders have had a tough schedule the last four games, but Sunday's loss to the Rams was disheartening. They trailed 28-6 before a fourth-quarter rally. The offense was particularly ineffective, which brought about more questions over the quarterback situation . Sunday's loss wasn't all Kirk Cousins' fault, but impatience over rookie Fernando Mendoza's first start was inevitable upon the first signs of trouble.

Head coach Klint Kubiak is a rookie at his job, and he could have shut down any quarterback speculation Sunday when asked. Instead he said the team was "thinking about everything," which invited a quarterback controversy. That lasted less than 24 hours. Kubiak made it clear Monday that Cousins would start. But he has invited weekly speculation on the issue.

"Eventually Fernando is going to play football, we have a plan but we don't have a timeline for that," Kubiak told the media Monday. "Kirk is playing really well, and we're in the hunt.

"Fernando is going to play at some point. It's not going to be this week."

The Texans' loss Sunday was one of the most damaging of the entire NFL season. They were double-digit favorites to beat the Giants, and a win over New York would have put Houston at 3-4, not far behind 4-2 Jacksonville with a head-to-head win over the Jaguars. And the Texans had a massive letdown in an overtime loss to the Giants. At 2-5, their margin of error is incredibly slim with 10 games to go.

At this point it's clear the Texans are nowhere near as good on defense as expected. They were 16th in defensive DVOA through Sunday's games and 24th in EPA ( expected points added ) allowed. Needing a stop in overtime Sunday, Houston allowed runs of 42 and 30 yards on back-to-back plays that ended the game.

"No magical elixir is going to drop out of the sky and ... fix it," Texans head coach DeMeco Ryans said according to AP. "We fix it by putting the work in and getting better at fundamentals of football and that's where we've got to just own it. As coaches, as players, we've all got to own it and we've got to find a way to turn this thing around."

There are still defensive problems. The Eagles, without several key starters on offense, including Jalen Hurts, moved the ball with ease on their first two drives that ended in touchdowns. But Dallas deserves credit for pitching a fourth-quarter shutout in a win it had to have. And the Cowboys' offense seems to be over whatever slump it was in.

Head coach Brian Schottenheimer challenged the offense to find balance, and it responded with 204 rushing yards on 5.4 yards per attempt on Monday night. If the Cowboys can run the ball like that, they'll have a few more 38-point games. And they might need those types of games, unless the defense's fourth-quarter performance is a sign of improvement.

The Falcons might be the toughest team in the NFL to figure out. Even if we discount the first two games, which Michael Penix Jr. missed, they have three impressive wins and two bad home losses. They're back on the upswing after beating the previously undefeated 49ers on Sunday. Even within the victory, we saw the best and worst of the Falcons. They fell behind 14-3, then outscored San Francisco 26-6 the rest of the game.

The star Sunday was rookie linebacker Kendal Daniels, who a week before was immobilized on the field and taken off on a stretcher after taking a knee to the head. He was back Sunday, with 11 tackles, a fumble recovery and an interception that practically clinched the win.

"I wasn't scared, but I definitely thought about it," Daniels said, via WSBTV . "I haven't been in full pads all week. What if I'm not OK? But once I got my first tackle in pregame, I was good."

Every team is allowed a mulligan or two over a long season, but what happened Sunday was atrocious from the Panthers. They trailed 43-6 at home to a Buccaneers team that had just one win beforehand. Carolina turned it over four times. It even had an extra point blocked and returned for 2 points . Bryce Young had by far his worst game of the season.

For a team that had shown signs of progress, it was bad. Even if it was just an off game, its run defense is a concern. Tampa Bay rushed for 258 yards. Carolina also gave up 291 rushing yards in the opener against Chicago.

"Obviously they found something today, and it's a copycat league, so we got to stop the bleeding because teams are going to watch this film and try to exploit any weaknesses in our defense," linebacker Bobby Okereke told the team's site .

There should be skepticism on the Giants, but Sunday was the type of win that will go a long way in a bad NFC East. The Giants were big underdogs at Houston but won in overtime, with J.J. McCarthy playing well in his first start and the running game coming alive .

The Giants face the Eagles and Commanders coming out of their Week 8 bye, two winnable games that could boost them to a huge lead in the division. Giants head coach John Harbaugh made quite a statement after the game, making it clear that after beating the Texans the Giants will be contenders in the division the rest of the way.

"The two most important games of the season will be coming up after we come back from the bye, which will set the direction for the rest of the season really," Harbaugh said, according to the team's site . "But we're going to be in this thing until the end now. This was a pivotal game. This was a really high-pressure game for our team. We didn't talk about that, but they all knew how important this game was, and they responded accordingly."

The Browns are on the kind of exciting run in close games that has rarely been seen in NFL history.

Cleveland got another last-second win when it responded to a game-tying touchdown by Tennessee with 58 seconds left by putting together a quick drive for the game-winning field goal as time expired. Pulling out close wins every week is unsustainable ("We're gonna have to figure out how to start faster. That's for damn sure," head coach Todd Monken said ), but a 5-2 record will keep the Browns in playoff contention. Odds are skeptical. DVOA has the Browns with just a 30% chance to make the playoffs. That's not stopping the good vibes.

"There's something about this group," Monken said, via the team's site . "There's something about those guys that play the next play and continue to fight for each other."

The NFL's officiating issues from early in the season hit a crescendo in Detroit on Sunday, when several questionable calls were made. The Packers lost 20-17 . They were outraged, and safety Xavier McKinney decided it was worth the fine to air out the officiating problem.

"I would rather get fined and try to help my team out because I see what's going on, and I see that it's killing us," McKinney said . "We all see it. We all see what's going on. Everybody sees what's going on, the fans see what's going on. … You're not even reviewing what you're calling. …

"Even they're looking at it, like, OK that's not it. I'm asking other refs and they're like, 'Oh, I'm not over there.' It's a lot of s*** that doesn't make sense right there."

Officiating or not, the Packers made key errors. Josh Jacobs was good in his return, but he dropped a pass in the end zone in the fourth quarter. Trey Smack missed two short field goals, one that was partially blocked right after Jacobs' drop. Matt LaFleur passed on a field goal to go for it on fourth-and-4 in the first half. Green Bay put up only 17 points on a bad Lions defense. And the officiating didn't help either.

Four of the Steelers' wins have come against losing teams (combined record: 9-19). They have won only one game by more than seven points, but they also have a victory over the Bengals and at some point it doesn't matter who the Steelers have beaten. They're 5-2 and going to be in playoff contention all season. They're making just enough plays, like they did to beat the 2-5 Saints on Sunday.

What might keep the Steelers going is the running back combination of Jaylen Warren, who has emerged as one of the best playmakers at the position this season, and Rico Dowdle, one of the best backups in the league. They had 223 of Pittsburgh's 343 yards on Sunday.

"Anytime we can just line up and give you Jaylen and Rico all day, that's a good day for us," Steelers head coach Mike McCarthy said, according to the team's site .

The Rams had their best game of the season Sunday. They let down a bit in the fourth quarter and gave the Raiders hope for a comeback, but the story was the 28-6 lead they built in the first half.

The Rams will be short on receivers, barring a much-needed trade, with Davante Adams out until perhaps late in the regular season. The offense might need to be reinvented as a run-first unit. We saw a bit of that Sunday. Kyren Williams rushed for 99 yards and a touchdown on 16 carries and Blake Corum had 93 yards and a touchdown (and had two others called back due to penalties) on 17 carries.

"That's a key factor for us," Rams head coach Sean McVay said via Rams Wire . "Any good offense that we've had here that I've been a part of, you've got to be able to do both."

It's unfair to just eliminate three long plays for a team and judge it on the rest of its production. Those explosive plays are earned. And the Broncos got a 62-yard touchdown run from Bo Nix, a 52-yard touchdown on a short pass to RJ Harvey and a 47-yard catch to Marvin Mims Jr. that set up a touchdown.

On the Broncos' other 53 plays, they gained only 216 yards. That's a middling 4 yards per play. Still, Sunday was another win. The Broncos are 5-2 and the Chiefs' loss on Sunday sets up a game that should frame the rest of the AFC West race as the Chiefs visit Denver in Week 8. The Broncos will have to find some consistency on offense and they have a few key injuries to track: receiver Jaylen Waddle has a chest injury, defensive lineman Zach Allen hurt his hamstring and cornerback Pat Surtain II has missed three straight games with an ankle injury.

Only two teams are worse than -5 in turnover differential . The Colts are last in the league at -9, and the Patriots are -7. It's impressive New England is above .500 given that mark. The other five teams at -4 or worse are under .500. The big turnover Thursday night that cost the Patriots dearly was a bad pass by Drake Maye into the end zone that was picked off by linebacker D'Marco Jackson. That was a big difference in a 30-24 loss at the Bears.

Maye played well other than that blemish. He had 321 passing yards and two touchdowns with that interception. One mistake swinging the game showed how slight the margins are in the NFL.

"Those plays, I talk about all the time, those plays that can swing the game, can impact the game," Maye said . "That was definitely one of them right there. I wish I definitely had that one back."

The Lions got a big win Sunday and a big return to the lineup. Safety Brian Branch was back after tearing his Achilles last season, and he had four tackles and an interception. He can make a big difference in a defense that needs the boost.

"That's just who he is, man," linebacker Derrick Barnes told MLive.com . "He a ballhawk, man. He run, he hits, man. He plays fast the whole game. That's who he is, man. And a lot of people feed off the energy."

Branch played 45 snaps, which was 67% of the Lions' defensive plays. That number will increase as he gets back to full strength. The Lions held the Packers to 17 points with Branch back in the lineup, which is progress from a unit that had struggled all season.

The Lamar Jackson situation is frustrating. The Ravens don't want Jackson to come back too soon and struggle playing through an injury, as he did last season, but they clearly needed him in a big game against the Bengals on Sunday. The Ravens did not score after halftime and lost 35-13 . It's the second straight week they were shut out in the second half and lost as a result.

Jackson practiced some last week and is seemingly close to a return. Baltimore's next two games are at the Bills and against the Jaguars. At the end of that, we'll know where the Ravens' season is headed. And if Jackson has returned to save it.

Brian Thomas Jr.'s playing time hasn't been above 62.4% in any game all season. Against Houston, before the bye, he played 15 snaps, including none in the second half. Over the Jaguars' last four games he has 25 yards. Yet, for some reason, Jaguars head coach Liam Coen predicted more for Thomas coming out of the bye.

"He's going to be able to help us make plays this week," Coen said, via Jags Wire . "I'd bet it, I know it."

Since Coen oversees decisions such as playing Thomas 15 snaps in the Jaguars' last game, that proclamation seems dubious. Thomas has been cut out of the offense, two years after he was a first-round draft pick and put up 1,282 yards as a rookie. It seems like he's a good bet to be dealt before the Nov. 10 trade deadline.

Seattle has risen to the top spot in defensive DVOA this season after a phenomenal performance against Kansas City. It shut down everything KC wanted to do, starting with Kenneth Walker III.

The problem for the Seahawks is they're 22nd on offense in DVOA. It's clear that the Seahawks have Jaxon Smith-Njigba and little else, although Emanuel Wilson did have 100 rushing yards and Zach Charbonnet is closing in on a return from a torn ACL. But no team needs a trade before the deadline more than Seattle, which has to find another playmaker.

The Bengals are in a great place at 4-2 after getting a really good road divisional win over the Ravens. You're about to hear more Joe Burrow MVP buzz soon, perhaps even this week. Burrow leads the NFL with a 71.7% completion percentage and has a career-best 110.4 passer rating. He has 1,653 yards, 15 touchdowns and three interceptions for a team that is now favored in betting markets to win the division. On Sunday, he had 249 yards and four touchdowns in the second half alone against Baltimore in a huge game for the Bengals' season. He also hasn't won MVP before, and voters like spreading the award around. It's surprising there hasn't been more talk about him creeping up on being the favorite.

"The second half, I think I was pretty lights out," Burrow said, via the team's transcripts.

The Bears have scored 30 or more points in three of Caleb Williams' four starts. The fourth was a surprising three-point effort against the Vikings, which probably says a lot about how good Minnesota's defense is this season. Chicago's offense might be just as good as Ben Johnson said it would be .

One thing that had been a question about Williams coming into the season was him missing too many passes. His completion percentage was 58.1% last season. He was one of two quarterbacks with on-target percentage of less than 70% last season, according to Pro Football Reference , and the other was J.J. McCarthy. This season, that has flipped. He has a completion percentage of 71%, just off the league lead. His on-target percentage is up to 79.6%, third in the NFL. He has gone from one of the most inaccurate quarterbacks to one of the most accurate in his third season. Williams has played just four games this season, but it appears he has arrived as one of the NFL's best QBs.

The Chiefs are allowed one bad game, in a hostile road environment against a great defense. They couldn't get anything going in a 20-3 loss . But it was troubling how little Kansas City did on offense once Kenneth Walker III was taken out of the equation. Walker had 36 rushing yards . Nobody else made an impact; no other Chief posted more than 44 yards.

Rashee Rice was out and that affected the offense. However, the Chiefs still have to be considered a candidate to make a trade for a receiver before the deadline to alleviate their recurring issues in the passing game.

"So you got to feel it on that plane ride home and understand that it sucks. But then how can you build off of it?" quarterback Patrick Mahomes said, via Chiefs Wire . "The biggest thing is as we get back and get back to that film study on the Broncos, you got to see where you made your mistakes and how they're going to try to execute, and then do stuff to combat that and play better. So, obviously, it sucks right now, but we'll be full steam ahead, trying to do our best to find a way to win this next week."

One side note to the Vikings' season is watching how J.J. McCarthy's time with the Giants plays out. So far, McCarthy has been very good. Less than one month after being traded to the Giants, McCarthy had 243 yards in just 11 minutes off the bench against the Saints in Week 6 and 252 yards in a mistake-free game against Houston, which New York won in overtime.

The Vikings gave McCarthy 10 starts, gave up on him, then traded the 2024 10th pick of the draft for a fifth-round selection. They did so while going all-in on Kyler Murray, who has been mostly underwhelming despite the team's great start to the season. And that came a year after allowing Sam Darnold to leave in free agency to Seattle, where he promptly won a Super Bowl. If McCarthy has a good season for the Giants, everyone will be examining how the Vikings couldn't make it work and why they jumped ship so quickly, for such little return on investment.

The Vikings could have been ranked ahead of the Bills. Minnesota hasn't lost yet, and its defense is far better than Buffalo's. The one factor in keeping the Bills at No. 2 is Josh Allen, who is adding 0.351 adjusted EPA per play, tops among quarterbacks with at least 150 snaps. No quarterback over the last two seasons has reached that mark, not even Allen in his 2024 MVP season. And Buffalo's results have been very good, with Allen carrying the team. The Bills' only loss was to a capable Patriots team that was desperate to save its season after a slow start.

The Bills' next game, after the bye, is hosting the Ravens on Sunday. It's unclear if Lamar Jackson will return for that one. Then they play at the Vikings on a Monday night in Week 9, which is a much better matchup than anyone could have anticipated when it was scheduled.

The bye is coming at a good time for the 49ers. One of the reasons Mike Evans, Deebo Samuel Sr., Nick Bosa and others might have been inactive Sunday was because the bye would give them an extra week of rest before their return. Niners tight end George Kittle was unwilling to use the injuries as an excuse for the loss to the Falcons.

"It's the NFL, injuries happen," Kittle told NBC Sports Bay Area . "It's just how much depth do you have, how many vets do you have that can stay healthy that can like continue to keep the elevation, like the standard of play up, you know, that's all that really matters."

articles.title: Dallas Cowboys beat spiralling Philadelphia Eagles as Dak Prescott and Javonte Williams star amid Jalen Hurts absence
articles.summary: Javonte Williams put up career-high numbers as the Dallas Cowboys beat the Philadelphia Eagles, who suffered their fifth straight defeat; Tanner McKee started at quarterback for the Eagles with Jalen Hurts set to miss the rest of the season due to blood clots in his lungs
articles.body:
Javonte Williams ran for a career-high 155 yards and a touchdown, and the Cowboys (3-4) remained in contention for the NFC East title. The New York Giants lead the division at 4-2-1.

The Eagles (2-5) are spiralling into a disaster of a season with their longest skid since 2016.

Philadelphia quarterback Jalen Hurts is expected to miss the rest of the season because of blood clots in his lungs.

Tanner McKee provided little encouragement that he can turn the season around, completing 23 of 35 passes for 211 yards with one touchdown and one interception. Prescott finished long drives with scores that McKee was unable to match.

With Dallas trailing 21-20 late in the third quarter, Lamb hauled in his second touchdown on a beautiful 16-yard floater from Prescott in the corner of the end zone. Prescott ran in the two-point conversion for a 28-21 lead.

Brandon Aubrey kicked field goals of 55, 27 and 24 yards. The final kick extended Dallas' lead to 31-21.

Williams capped the scoring and the first 150-yard rushing game by a Dallas player since Ezekiel Elliott in 2018 with a 2-yard touchdown. The Cowboys finished with 204 yards rushing.

McKee had a pass intercepted by linebacker DeMarvion Overshown late in the fourth. McKee orchestrated the first Eagles' touchdown drive in the third quarter this season when they ran almost 10 minutes off the clock and he hit rookie Makai Lemon for a 4-yard touchdown and a 21-20 lead.

The Eagles didn't score again and are running out of time to salvage their season.

The Cowboys got a field goal on the opening drive, and the Eagles came right back and made it 7-3 on Saquon Barkley's eight-yard touchdown run. Barkley returned after missing the last two-plus games with a hamstring injury and had 37 yards rushing on the drive.

Barkley entered with 36 yards rushing all season. He still seemed bothered by the hamstring and had to visit the sideline medical tent. Barkley also missed long stretches getting treatment for his back on the sideline and finished with 62 yards on seven carries.

Prescott threw touchdown passes of nine yards to Lamb and 21 yards to George Pickens that helped the Cowboys stretch their lead to 20-14 at halftime. Pickens' catch was particularly impressive, as he escaped tight coverage by safety Andrew Mukuba in the back of the end zone and dragged his left foot sideways for the score.

articles.title: Colin Kaepernick: Why I would do it all again despite it costing my career
articles.summary: In his first interview with BBC Sport since taking the knee for the first time, Colin Kaepernick reflects on his journey.
articles.body:
Ten years on from making the gesture that catapulted him to iconic status, but which he believes led to his exile from the sport he loved, Colin Kaepernick insists he has no regrets.

It was September 2016 when NFL star Kaepernick knelt during the US national anthem before a match as a peaceful protest against racial injustice and police brutality.

It proved both inspirational and divisive.

In his first interview with BBC Sport since then, Kaepernick reflects on his journey; his pride at seeing England footballers take the knee, athlete activism, the relationship between sport and politics, and the price he paid for being a figurehead for the civil rights movement.

"I knew the protest could potentially cost me my career," he says. "History shows us…that is a reality for athletes.

"We also see this in broader movements, going well beyond costing someone their career, and costing people their lives. We see Malcolm X assassinated, we see MLK [Martin Luther King] assassinated, so the consequences are real."

Having initially sat to protest against the plight of black people in the US, Kaepernick first knelt during the Star-Spangled Banner before his San Francisco 49ers team played a pre-season game. It was an act he would repeat before 11 regular-season contests that year.

At the time, he said he could not stand up for - and show pride in - a flag "for a country that oppresses black people and people of colour", adding: "This is bigger than football and it would be selfish on my part to look the other way."

His stance against racial inequality was seen as heroic by many, inspiring other NFL players to follow suit. But there was also condemnation from those who said it was disrespectful to the military.

Those dissenting voices included Donald Trump - then a presidential candidate.

Trump described the act as "a terrible thing" and unpatriotic. He even suggested Kaepernick should find another country to live in, adding players who refused to stand for the national anthem should be fired.

The NFL said it would fine teams whose players did not stand.

Kaepernick opted out of his contract with the 49ers in March 2017, though the club's management later said he would have been released regardless.

Despite leading the 49ers to the 2013 Super Bowl, and throwing 16 touchdowns in his final season, one of the most talented quarterbacks in the sport never found a new team.

Speaking from New York, Kaepernick says he anticipated the reaction to taking the knee. "What I couldn't have predicted was the people who would show up for me in significant ways, and also the people who worked against me and against the movement," he adds.

Kaepernick eventually filed a grievance against NFL team owners, who he believed had conspired not to hire him because of his protests, reaching a financial settlement in 2019.

That year, the NFL arranged a private workout for Kaepernick, but he chose not to attend, instead holding his own session elsewhere to allow media to be present. Hopes of a comeback never materialised.

The NFL later admitted it was "wrong for not listening to players earlier", and encouraged "all to speak out and peacefully protest".

Colin Kaepernick speaks to BBC's Dan Roan

Former NFL quarterback Colin Kaepernick gives his first interview with BBC Sport, 10 years on from making the gesture that catapulted him to iconic status

'Humbling to see England players take knee'

Following the murder of George Floyd while in police custody in Minneapolis in 2020, taking the knee became a feature of Black Lives Matter protests, and widespread across sport.

England's men's and women's football teams were among those to follow suit.

"That was a surprising moment for me," says Kaepernick.

"I did think about the protest going beyond the US and how that may show up in other countries. To be able to see the national teams going out and protesting, it was humbling. I was happy that they were doing it.

"I also know there's still a lot of work to be done within racism in the UK and more broadly. And this is a global challenge that we are collectively fighting against.

"I was very excited to be able to see players actively calling that out, and willing to begin taking action towards addressing it."

Despite keeping a relatively low profile for most of the past decade, Kaepernick remains a standard-bearer for the civil rights movement.

But while surveys suggest the vast majority of professional athletes intend to use their social media channels to raise awareness about racial injustice , external , he accepts the momentum behind athlete activism seems to have slowed in recent years.

It was notable that several players across five clubs chose to remain standing when Premier League players took the knee as part of October's No Room for Racism campaign.

Anti-discrimination campaign group Kick It Out told BBC Sport the gesture "still has value in raising awareness of the structural inequalities that exist in football and society", but added it could "understand the reasons players might become frustrated with the pace of change".

Reports of discrimination received by the charity more than doubled in the past five years, reaching record levels last season.

"I think we're in a moment that demands protests more than ever," says Kaepernick.

"Why I think protests are not as loud right now [is] because of the concerted efforts that have been taken by organisations like the NFL, like the Trump administration, and corporate entities following along and capitulating in that process.

"While those things are happening, I think the reality of the state of the US, and more broadly the world, demands that we show up in a more significant way."

Kaepernick is all too familiar with how polarising it can be to take a political stand in sport.

Opponents of taking the knee have claimed it is a political and divisive statement, and that rather than demonstrating backing for the Black Lives Matter movement , it has shown support for the organisation of the same name.

In 2018, critics encouraged people to destroy Nike goods after the sportswear giant used Kaepernick as the face of an advertising campaign featuring the caption 'Believe in something. Even if it means sacrificing everything.'

So what does he say to those who argue that sport and politics should be kept apart?

"They ring hollow and feel very hypocritical, because politics is inherently part of sports," he says.

"We see within [American] football, we see taxpayers funding NFL stadiums. We see our NFL owners going out and supporting political candidates... so to try to position this as if sports aren't political, in many ways feels just laughable to me, and disconnected.

"Now, where the question comes in for people is: 'We don't want the athletes to be political. Everything around them can be political, but the athletes themselves, we don't want them to have a voice in the politics, because that interrupts our entertainment and our ability to disconnect.' For me, that's where society has a challenge with it."

Having encountered significant opposition from high-profile athletes during his first term, Trump seems to have encountered less challenge from the world of sport during his second, notably becoming the first sitting US president to attend the Super Bowl.

He has also appeared at golf's Ryder Cup, and the finals of football's Club World Cup and World Cup, though he was also booed when attending the NBA Finals in New York in June.

"It ties into the conversation of 'are sports political?' when he is going out and actively trying to use them to gain favour and popularity", says Kaepernick, adding that Fifa's controversial decision to award the US President its inaugural 'Peace Prize' last year was "regrettable".

"The part that I think is great to see is when he's showing up to these events and getting booed by the crowd, which speaks to the political environment that he's created, that the majority of the country does not agree with…when it comes to sports, people need to continue to respond accordingly."

Now 38, Kaepernick has published a memoir titled The Perilous Fight, detailing his childhood in California having been adopted by a white family, encountering racism, and his education and evolution. "People saw the moment. But they didn't see the years that made it possible", he says. "The questions about who I was; the injustices I could no longer ignore; the voices of those who came before me that I carried into that stadium...When I took a knee, it wasn't a sudden act. It was the result of years of becoming."

So how did he find the process of reliving his journey?

"Are there moments that are challenging going back to? Yes. But I hope that insight helps other people navigate situations...that helps them move forward or helps them to go accomplish things."

Kaepernick also supports community organisations via his Know Your Rights education campaign, is a philanthropist, and has written a number of children's books.

Even now, he maintains the fitness regime he had during his time at the 49ers, just in case an unlikely opportunity to resume his NFL career arises.

Kaepernick may not have thrown a ball in anger for almost a decade, but he is widely regarded as one of the most significant athletes in modern history.

The way he used his platform to promote change has been compared to legendary boxer Muhammad Ali's support of the anti-war movement, and US athletes Tommie Smith and John Carlos giving the Black Power Salute at the 1968 Olympics.

"To even be in the same conversation with the likes of [them], is extremely humbling," he says. "But more importantly, I just try to stay focused on the work.

"What can we do to help people? And how do we collectively move forward as a society? And, ultimately, how we build a society that works for everybody. That feels like a very simple principle that has been lost.

"I know in the US specifically, we have a lot of work to do there. I hope we begin taking the steps to get back to a place where we are actually addressing people's needs. And create a society that is equitable for everyone."

articles.title: Super Bowl 2027: Jay-Z to headline Super Bowl LXI half-time show at SoFi Stadium in Los Angeles
articles.summary: Jay-Z picks himself to headline the Super Bowl LXI half-time show on February 14 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California; the 25-time Grammy Award-winning rapper follows on from the likes of Kendrick Lamar, Michael Jackson, Coldplay and Rihanna in leading the NFL's showpiece entertainment
articles.body:
The rapper's Roc Nation entertainment company has been in partnership with the NFL to produce the Super Bowl half-time show since 2019 - seven years on, it is his turn.

The Super Bowl heads to SoFi Stadium, home of the Los Angeles Rams and Chargers, on Sunday February 14, live on Sky Sports NFL.

"From Reasonable Doubt to standing on the Super Bowl Halftime stage, this has been a journey," stated Jay-Z. "Thirty years of music, work, and culture on the world's biggest stage. This run continues to be a dream come true."

This year has marked a celebration of "JAY-Z 30" three decades on from his debut album Reasonable Doubt, resulting in attendance records at sold-out concerts at Yankee Stadium as well as in London, Paris and Los Angeles.

The 25-time Grammy Award winner, whose 89 nominations are second only in history to his wife Beyonce, is the first hip-hop artist to be inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame.

"For several years, we've had the privilege of working closely with JAŸ-Z and Roc Nation, and I've seen the extraordinary impact he has had on the Super Bowl half-time Show," said NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell.

"When we first reached an agreement with Roc Nation to produce the show, I had just one request: that JAŸ-Z take the stage himself one day, whenever the moment felt right to him. I couldn't be more excited for fans around the world to experience the artistry, creativity and cultural impact he will bring to the Super Bowl stage."

Last year's Super Bowl saw Bad Bunny make history as the first ever Latino solo artist to headline the half-time show as he performed at Levi's Stadium in Santa Clara.

The year before saw Kendrick Lamar's performance in New Orleans become the most watched Super Bowl half-time show in history.

articles.title: ‘It’s not like he’s naive’: As Cowboys hear Brian Schottenheimer criticism, they’re not content to just beat injury-riddled Eagles
articles.summary: The Cowboys coach's postgame press conference was far terser than usual, perhaps not coincidentally amid the criticism he’s received and the questions about...
articles.body:
PHILADELPHIA — Walking from the floodlit grass of Lincoln Financial Field back to the visiting locker room that vibrated with celebratory music, Dallas Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheimer revealed no expression.

Schottenheimer didn't cheer nor smile as he walked with purpose toward the locker room. Neither would Dak Prescott minutes later, even as the quarterback who threw for three touchdowns in the Cowboys' 38-21 win over the Philadelphia Eagles passed teammates ready for high-fives or embraces.

"I just expect that," Prescott said of the win. "Obviously I've been in the league 11 years now and understanding where this team is, what we need to do, the importance."

Prescott spoke similarly when asked if the Cowboys' 200+ yards rushing and 200+ yards passing represented the most complete offensive game of 3-4 Dallas' season.

"The numbers would say so, but this is one game," Prescott said. "We've got to build on this so that we can continue to do this. So we're not going to be complacent and say, 'This is it.' We've got to go get better this week and do it again next week."

Perhaps the Cowboys leaders' muted tones, if not outward humility, sound like a change from the "GOTI" acronym they touted during training camp for the "Greatest Offense There Is," with Prescott and Co. also speaking openly then about their Super Bowl visions . But to Prescott and at least some others, "GOTI" was not a pronouncement that the roster had arrived at deserving the praise. It was a challenge to teammates that their roster was assembled in a way suggesting they could be the greatest ever.

Consecutive prime-time losses to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers (starting undrafted rookie Jalon Daniels in place of Baker Mayfield) and the Green Bay Packers began to cloud Dallas' upside and control of playoff hopes. Schottenheimer has led the charge in shifting his tone in at least some ways.

Sure, a 17-point road division win matters. And "absolutely" was Prescott willing to deem Monday night a must-win game. But beating a team that's lost half a dozen offensive starters won't be sufficient to make the type of playoff run for which the Cowboys hope. Scoring 35+ points only against the Commanders and Eagles after they'd lost Jayden Daniels (elbow) and Jalen Hurts (blood clots) respectively doesn't warrant crowning as the offense to fear.

Consider Schottenheimer aware of the criticism some are leveling against his play-calling, game management and team organizing. Consider the Cowboys eager to prove it all wrong.

Monday night was a "definitely hungry, pissed-off version of Schotty," Prescott said. "It's not like he's naive. It's not like he hadn't heard some noise about him and whether it's calling the games or whatever doubt that's been out there. But we've got his back. He knows that. ….

"More importantly, it's just about us going out there and executing on Sundays."

Cowboys re-commit to run after they'd 'gotten away from it a little earlier' in consecutive losses

Against an Eagles team down Hurts, wide receiver DeVonta Smith and wide receiver Dontayvion Wicks, the Cowboys' defense still allowed touchdowns on Philadelphia's first two drives. Running back Saquon Barkley, battling a hamstring injury and then compensatory back injury, gashed the Cowboys for 62 yards and a touchdown on just seven carries.

So Prescott and Co. knew they needed to score early and often to spell their defensive counterparts.

On six of their first seven possessions, they did.

Dallas' star wideouts, CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens, accounted for 131 yards and three touchdowns combined. A key to their success: Dallas' season-high 38 carries.

After 13 and 15 total rushes vs. the Bucs and Packers respectively, Dallas committed to the run game against Philadelphia.

The result: No longer were the Cowboys an offense unable to handle the blitz or balance their run-pass menu. Dallas ran six times in its first-quarter touchdown drive to set up Prescott to a spinning Lamb for the initial score.

A methodical, 14-play drive in the second quarter continued to incorporate some runs even as the explosive touchdown came courtesy a toe-dragging George Pickens 21-yard catch near the right boundary of the end zone.

Only once before the fourth quarter would a Cowboys run play exceed 15 yards. But the carries gradually wore down an Eagles defense with little room for error, demanding defenders return to the box rather than only focus on Lamb and Pickens.

Avoiding an early hole helped Dallas run the ball. But so did simply deciding to commit to running the ball.

"Not being stubborn, but saying, 'Hey, we're going to run the ball. We're going to make this pop. We're going to make this happen one way or another,'" Prescott told Yahoo Sports after the game. "And Schotty may attest to it: I think in the past couple of weeks we might have even gotten away from it a little earlier than we wanted to. It doesn't help when you're down and you don't feel like you're necessarily stopping them. But yeah, it's a big difference when you're not down multiple scores and you can stick to it even when runs are inefficient.

All three of Prescott's touchdowns targeted his receivers near the outer edges of the end zone in order to reduce the chances a defender tipped or intercepted the ball, as had plagued the Cowboys four times in the prior two games. Lamb spun away from Eagles defensive back Cooper DeJean on the first score, Pickens extending past safety Andrew Mukuba on the second.

"They did a good job of still trying to play over the top and taking that away, clouding George and rerouting CeeDee here and there when they could," Prescott said. "They blitzed us early. We had the answers for it, and that allowed us to stay balanced all throughout the game."

The threat of big receiving plays helped running back Javonte Williams and the offensive line establish the run to the tune of his career-high 155 yards.

"We got a high-level, high-power offense," Williams said. "When you got GP, CeeDee, [tight end] Jake Ferguson, those guys on the outside? I mean, it's going to open up the running."

With NFC East attainable and questions loud, what is Cowboys' mindset?

Improving to 3-4, the Cowboys now sit second in the NFC East and 1.5 games behind the 4-2-1 New York Giants.

Outside of a Nov. 15 game against the 6-1 San Francisco 49ers, the Cowboys' coming slate consists of below-.500 teams in the 2-5 Arizona Cardinals, 2-5 Indianapolis Colts, 1-6 Tennessee Titans and (again) the 2-5 Eagles.

There is opportunity. And there is also noise to shut out.

"It was very important that we get this win, to be honest. One, for the division and what we want to do at the end of the year, and two, for our confidence," Lamb said after tallying a game-high 74 receiving yards and two touchdowns. "Losing two games we felt like we could've and should've won — I hate living in that 'could've-should've-would've' world, but I feel like we could have won those games but it didn't work out for us.

"Tonight we got it done and we're on to better things."

Just before boarding the bus, Prescott reflected on the worlds his coaches and teammates live in, the range of criticisms they have and haven't heard lately, and how it's impacted the building.

"It doesn't bother me, but I see the way that it affects other people, and that bothers me," Prescott told Yahoo Sports of the negativity surrounding a Cowboys team underperforming relative to expectation. "And you can't always protect people from taking in the information or hearing the noise. I can control what I hear. I can control what I read. Not everybody's the same way. …

"Some people want to read it or want to listen to it for motivation and then you hear so much and you're pissed off about it."

Prescott emphasized that "I don't blame" nor "get upset" with coaches or teammates impacted by criticism. Was Schottenheimer among those after the offense he coordinated managed just 10 and then 7 points entering the fourth quarter the prior two games? His postgame press conference was far terser than usual, perhaps not coincidentally amid the criticism he's received and the questions about his confidence.

This Cowboys' offense, with a healthy offensive line to complement weapons like Prescott, Lamb and Pickens, did not enter the season with expectations of neutrality. The offense entered the season with an expectation of greatness that emanated from within and without, a product of the continuity and high-end talent invested — and also of necessity.

Rarely do first-time play-callers overhauling personnel and scheme in an organization find immediate rhythm and success. The Cowboys had hoped a potent offense could take the pressure off Christian Parker's defense to perform immediately, recognizing that early in the season some players may be prone to overthink their new and diverse set of responsibilities.

Committing to the run game is necessary for the defense, too, with Dallas needing to control the clock to spell its defense that struggles to get off the field. Also key: avoiding turnovers. The Cowboys have won the turnover battle just twice in seven tries — each time, they've scored more than 35 points (albeit against teams down a starting quarterback).

Can Dallas string together just their second winning steak of the Schottenheimer era? At home against the Cardinals on Sunday, they'll have the chance to try.

"We say the division's right in front of us — it is as long as we win. …" Prescott said. "Momentum's real, especially in this league. Yeah, especially in what we do and just understanding the parity and how tough this league is. When you get a win, the confidence it gives your group, the confidence it gives this team and just being able to build off of that and the benefit of also going home …

"So it's Arizona, right? And we just got to make sure you have a great week of preparations to make sure that translates into a big win. And from there, you get two in a row, you start stacking."

articles.title: NFL trade deadline: Chargers' Khalil Mack linked to two NFC powerhouse teams
articles.summary: Should the Los Angeles Chargers move on from Khalil Mack, two NFC teams could be interested in acquiring him.
articles.body:
With the trade deadline approaching, the 49ers and Bears are expected to be highly active, and the rumor mill has linked them to Chargers edge rusher Khalil Mack.

For the Bears, trading for Mack would be the ultimate full-circle moment. Mack previously spent four strong seasons in Chicago (2018–2021). Adding Mack alongside Montez Sweat would instantly give the Bears one of the NFL's most formidable edge-rushing duos.

While the 49ers hold a strong lead in the NFC West, injuries have hurt their defensive front, most notably the loss of Nick Bosa to a calf injury in Week 2. The defense ranks 24th in the league in pressure rate. Adding Mack would aid that department as San Francisco looks to make another deep run.

Even though the 35-year-old Mack has shown he still has juice, he is in the final year of an expiring contract, and moving on from him to accumulate future draft assets should be a higher priority, given they are currently 0-6, a playoff berth looks unlikely.

The Bolts could likely land a fourth- or fifth-round pick for Mack.

articles.title: Jeremiah Smith makes too much sense for Chargers in 2027 NFL Draft
articles.summary: The Chargers are urged to go after the No. 1 pick and select Ohio State wide receiver Jeremiah Smith.
articles.body:
The Chargers are on pace to grab the No. 1 overall pick in the 2027 NFL Draft.

That wasn't part of the Chargers' plans entering the season; however, that's been the case through their first six games. Los Angeles sits at 0-6 and is right in the thick of the race for the No. 1 pick.

While the Chargers are convinced that they'll turn things around and do what they can to salvage the 2026 season, it may be best for them to roll over, become sellers before the trade deadline, and shoot for the top pick, all so they can potentially draft Ohio State wide receiver Jeremiah Smith .

Potentially adding Smith alongside Justin Herbert could do wonders for the Chargers' offense next season. Not only could he provide an immediate boost, but Smith could also give Los Angeles a dimension it has lacked since Mike Williams.

"Jeremiah Smith can be the X wideout the Los Angeles Chargers failed to replace," Noah Furtado of The Athletic wrote .

"And with the Chargers 0-6 and holding the No. 1 draft spot at the bye, it looks possible they could get the Ohio State standout receiver in April."

Smith is the nation's best player. His elite size, speed, and wide receiver skill set are second to none, and like Williams, Smith excels at 50/50 balls.

He stands at 6-foot-4 and weighs roughly 225 pounds. Everything about him screams "elite," and with this year's quarterback class not looking too bright, Smith has the tools to be the first player taken.

Smith would immediately be the Chargers' true "X" receiver and red-zone weapon. His presence and skillset alone would bolster the wide receiver room.

On top of that, Smith would ease the pressure off Herbert, who has lacked a true star to throw to for the past three seasons.

The Chargers acquiring Smith would be a step in the right direction; however, it wouldn't solve the deeper issues that plague the team.

The No. 1 pick is certainly in the realm of possibility for the Chargers. However, it remains to be seen whether they will embrace that possibility coming out of their bye week.

articles.title: LAURA RUTLEDGE IS TAKING OVER SPORTS MEDIA AND NFL FANS ARE LOVING IT
articles.summary: There are big names in sports media. There are household names. And then there is Laura Rutledge, who seems to be everywhere sports fans turn these days. NFL...
articles.body:
There are big names in sports media. There are household names. And then there is Laura Rutledge, who seems to be everywhere sports fans turn these days.

NFL Live? She's there. Monday Night Football? She's there. College football's biggest stages? She's there, too.

At this point, ESPN might as well give Laura Rutledge her own channel.

Because whether fans are watching NFL coverage during the week or tuning in for a massive primetime matchup, Rutledge has become one of the faces they recognize immediately.

And the best part? She has earned that visibility by doing the work.

Rutledge joined ESPN in 2014 and has steadily expanded her role across the network.

She became the host of NFL Live in 2020, spent a decade helping make SEC Nation a staple of college football Saturdays and took on a full-time Monday Night Football sideline reporting role in 2025.

Now, she is part of ESPN's preparations for its first-ever Super Bowl broadcast in February 2027.

Her responsibilities span daily studio coverage, live game reporting, major college football events and the NFL's biggest moments. Few broadcasters have a portfolio that crosses so many major assignments.

ESPN clearly trusts her to handle the spotlight.

THE VIRAL MOMENTS ARE ONLY PART OF THE STORY

Remember when Rutledge went viral for sprinting across the field at the Sugar Bowl to make it to her halftime hosting duties?

It was a perfect snapshot of the job: live television, a tight deadline and a reporter moving at full speed to get where she needed to be.

But reducing Rutledge to viral clips misses the bigger picture.

She prepares for interviews, navigates live broadcasts and handles the pressure of covering athletes and coaches immediately after emotionally charged games. Her work requires more than a familiar face and a microphone.

It takes preparation, composure and the ability to ask meaningful questions when the cameras are rolling.

That is why her growing presence matters.

IS SHE ESPN'S MOST VALUABLE ON-AIR PERSONALITY?

Now comes the debate that could get sports media fans arguing.

Stephen A. Smith has the debate-show spotlight. Scott Van Pelt has his signature late-night presence. Pat McAfee brings a completely different energy to sports television.

She can move from a studio discussion to an NFL sideline and then into the biggest moments of the college football calendar. Her appeal is built on versatility, credibility and a broadcasting style that works across multiple audiences.

And she is doing it at a time when ESPN continues to invest in personalities who can connect with viewers across different platforms.

Calling her the biggest name in all of sports media is debatable. But arguing that she belongs in the conversation about ESPN's most recognizable and versatile broadcasters is much harder to dismiss.

THE NEXT CHAPTER COULD BE HER BIGGEST YET

Rutledge's departure from SEC Nation after the 2025 season was not the end of her college football story. It was a shift toward an even broader portfolio of assignments.

With NFL Live, Monday Night Football and major-event coverage on her schedule, she has a chance to become an even more familiar face to sports fans nationwide.

The Super Bowl stage in February could be another defining moment.

And if ESPN continues placing her in its biggest broadcasts, do not be surprised if her profile keeps growing.

Laura Rutledge is no longer just a familiar face on SEC Saturdays. She is one of the central figures in ESPN's sports coverage — and she may be entering the biggest stretch of her career.

So let's settle it: Is Laura Rutledge the biggest name in sports media right now, or does someone else still own that crown?

articles.title: ‘He Can’t Take It to Egregious Levels’ — Tom Brady’s Criticism of Officials on FOX Is ‘Drawing Attention’ Given NFL’s Restrictions on Raiders Owner
articles.summary: Tom Brady had plenty to say about the flags during Sunday’s Green Bay Packers-Detroit Lions game. His ownership stake makes those complaints a little more co...
articles.body:
Tom Brady had plenty to say about the flags during Sunday's Green Bay Packers-Detroit Lions game. His ownership stake makes those complaints a little more complicated.

The FOX analyst questioned several officiating decisions during Detroit's 20–17 victory, bringing fresh attention to the limits attached to his role with the Las Vegas Raiders. Calling a penalty questionable is one thing the league allows him to do. How heated that criticism can get remains a judgment call.

Mark Maske Explains the Limit on Tom Brady's Officiating Criticism

Front Office Sports reporter Mark Maske highlighted that distinction after Brady's commentary became a talking point.

"The NFL's restrictions on Brady, stemming from his role as a Raiders part-owner, include a limitation on how far he can go in criticizing the officiating. It's subjective," Maske wrote .

"But the indication always has been that Brady can criticize a call that's made during a game in his Fox role, but he can't take it to egregious levels."

Maske's explanation leaves room for Brady to disagree with what viewers are seeing. It also means an animated objection doesn't automatically establish that he broke a league rule.

Sunday gave Brady several opportunities to test that balance. The Green Bay Packers were penalized for roughing Jared Goff on separate plays involving Brenton Cox Jr. and Karl Brooks. Brady's objections to the roughing calls became part of a broadcast in which the officiating drew considerable scrutiny.

On the late flag against Brooks, Brady sounded baffled.

"No, my goodness! What is that?" he said. "You can't keep tacking on 15 yards."

FOX rules analyst Dean Blandino supported his assessment of that tackle. Ryan Glasspiegel's report noted that Brady's objections focused on individual plays, which could matter when evaluating whether he crossed the league's line.

PREDICT THE NFL SEASON: PFN's Free NFL Playoff Predictor

Brady's Dual Role Keeps His Broadcast Comments Under a Microscope

There is precedent for the NFL allowing Brady to challenge a decision without punishing him.

In November 2024, he questioned Brian Branch's ejection during another Packers-Lions matchup. The league took no disciplinary action. NFL spokesperson Brian McCarthy explained then that its concern involved excessive criticism or comments questioning an official's integrity.

That earlier decision helps explain why Sunday's comments alone don't establish a violation. It also puts the focus on what Brady actually said about the calls.

Glasspiegel reported Monday that FOX declined to comment and the NFL had not immediately responded to a request for comment. His report did not announce a fine or other punishment stemming from Sunday's broadcast.

The awkwardness is built into Brady's two jobs. FOX viewers expect a candid explanation when a replay makes a penalty difficult to understand. His ownership role subjects those explanations to an additional standard.

Brady can call out a flag. The lingering question is how forcefully he can do it before the NFL throws one his way.

articles.title: 'I would do it again' - Kaepernick reflects on price of protest, 10 years on
articles.summary: In his first interview with BBC Sport since taking the knee for the first time, Colin Kaepernick reflects on his journey.
articles.body:
Ten years on from making the gesture that catapulted him to iconic status, but which he believes led to his exile from the sport he loved, Colin Kaepernick insists he has no regrets.

It was September 2016 when NFL star Kaepernick knelt during the US national anthem before a match as a peaceful protest against racial injustice and police brutality.

It proved both inspirational and divisive.

In his first interview with BBC Sport since then, Kaepernick reflects on his journey; his pride at seeing England footballers take the knee, athlete activism, the relationship between sport and politics, and the price he paid for being a figurehead for the civil rights movement.

"I knew the protest could potentially cost me my career," he says. "History shows us…that is a reality for athletes.

"We also see this in broader movements, going well beyond costing someone their career, and costing people their lives. We see Malcolm X assassinated, we see MLK [Martin Luther King] assassinated, so the consequences are real."

Having initially sat to protest against the plight of black people in the US, Kaepernick first knelt during the Star-Spangled Banner before his San Francisco 49ers team played a pre-season game. It was an act he would repeat before 11 regular-season contests that year.

At the time, he said he could not stand up for - and show pride in - a flag "for a country that oppresses black people and people of colour", adding: "This is bigger than football and it would be selfish on my part to look the other way."

His stance against racial inequality was seen as heroic by many, inspiring other NFL players to follow suit. But there was also condemnation from those who said it was disrespectful to the military.

Those dissenting voices included Donald Trump - then a presidential candidate.

Trump described the act as "a terrible thing" and unpatriotic. He even suggested Kaepernick should find another country to live in, adding players who refused to stand for the national anthem should be fired.

The NFL said it would fine teams whose players did not stand.

Kaepernick opted out of his contract with the 49ers in March 2017, though the club's management later said he would have been released regardless.

Despite leading the 49ers to the 2013 Super Bowl, and throwing 16 touchdowns in his final season, one of the most talented quarterbacks in the sport never found a new team.

Speaking from New York, Kaepernick says he anticipated the reaction to taking the knee. "What I couldn't have predicted was the people who would show up for me in significant ways, and also the people who worked against me and against the movement," he adds.

Kaepernick eventually filed a grievance against NFL team owners, who he believed had conspired not to hire him because of his protests, reaching a financial settlement in 2019.

That year, the NFL arranged a private workout for Kaepernick, but he chose not to attend, instead holding his own session elsewhere to allow media to be present. Hopes of a comeback never materialised.

The NFL later admitted it was "wrong for not listening to players earlier", and encouraged "all to speak out and peacefully protest".

'Humbling to see England players take knee'

Following the murder of George Floyd while in police custody in Minneapolis in 2020, taking the knee became a feature of Black Lives Matter protests, and widespread across sport.

England's men's and women's football teams were among those to follow suit.

"That was a surprising moment for me," says Kaepernick.

"I did think about the protest going beyond the US and how that may show up in other countries. To be able to see the national teams going out and protesting, it was humbling. I was happy that they were doing it.

"I also know there's still a lot of work to be done within racism in the UK and more broadly. And this is a global challenge that we are collectively fighting against.

"I was very excited to be able to see players actively calling that out, and willing to begin taking action towards addressing it."

Despite keeping a relatively low profile for most of the past decade, Kaepernick remains a standard-bearer for the civil rights movement.

But while surveys suggest the vast majority of professional athletes intend to use their social media channels to raise awareness about racial injustice , he accepts the momentum behind athlete activism seems to have slowed in recent years.

It was notable that several players across five clubs chose to remain standing when Premier League players took the knee as part of October's No Room for Racism campaign.

Anti-discrimination campaign group Kick It Out told BBC Sport the gesture "still has value in raising awareness of the structural inequalities that exist in football and society", but added it could "understand the reasons players might become frustrated with the pace of change".

Reports of discrimination received by the charity more than doubled in the past five years, reaching record levels last season.

"I think we're in a moment that demands protests more than ever," says Kaepernick.

"Why I think protests are not as loud right now [is] because of the concerted efforts that have been taken by organisations like the NFL, like the Trump administration, and corporate entities following along and capitulating in that process.

"While those things are happening, I think the reality of the state of the US, and more broadly the world, demands that we show up in a more significant way."

Kaepernick is all too familiar with how polarising it can be to take a political stand in sport.

Opponents of taking the knee have claimed it is a political and divisive statement, and that rather than demonstrating backing for the Black Lives Matter movement , it has shown support for the organisation of the same name.

In 2018, critics encouraged people to destroy Nike goods after the sportswear giant used Kaepernick as the face of an advertising campaign featuring the caption 'Believe in something. Even if it means sacrificing everything.'

So what does he say to those who argue that sport and politics should be kept apart?

"They ring hollow and feel very hypocritical, because politics is inherently part of sports," he says.

"We see within [American] football, we see taxpayers funding NFL stadiums. We see our NFL owners going out and supporting political candidates... so to try to position this as if sports aren't political, in many ways feels just laughable to me, and disconnected.

"Now, where the question comes in for people is: 'We don't want the athletes to be political. Everything around them can be political, but the athletes themselves, we don't want them to have a voice in the politics, because that interrupts our entertainment and our ability to disconnect.' For me, that's where society has a challenge with it."

Having encountered significant opposition from high-profile athletes during his first term, Trump seems to have encountered less challenge from the world of sport during his second, notably becoming the first sitting US president to attend the Super Bowl.

He has also appeared at golf's Ryder Cup, and the finals of football's Club World Cup and World Cup, though he was also booed when attending the NBA Finals in New York in June.

"It ties into the conversation of 'are sports political?' when he is going out and actively trying to use them to gain favour and popularity", says Kaepernick, adding that Fifa's controversial decision to award the US President its inaugural 'Peace Prize' last year was "regrettable".

"The part that I think is great to see is when he's showing up to these events and getting booed by the crowd, which speaks to the political environment that he's created, that the majority of the country does not agree with…when it comes to sports, people need to continue to respond accordingly."

Now 38, Kaepernick has published a memoir titled The Perilous Fight, detailing his childhood in California having been adopted by a white family, encountering racism, and his education and evolution. "People saw the moment. But they didn't see the years that made it possible", he says. "The questions about who I was; the injustices I could no longer ignore; the voices of those who came before me that I carried into that stadium...When I took a knee, it wasn't a sudden act. It was the result of years of becoming."

So how did he find the process of reliving his journey?

"Are there moments that are challenging going back to? Yes. But I hope that insight helps other people navigate situations...that helps them move forward or helps them to go accomplish things."

Kaepernick also supports community organisations via his Know Your Rights education campaign, is a philanthropist, and has written a number of children's books.

Even now, he maintains the fitness regime he had during his time at the 49ers, just in case an unlikely opportunity to resume his NFL career arises.

Kaepernick may not have thrown a ball in anger for almost a decade, but he is widely regarded as one of the most significant athletes in modern history.

The way he used his platform to promote change has been compared to legendary boxer Muhammad Ali's support of the anti-war movement, and US athletes Tommie Smith and John Carlos giving the Black Power Salute at the 1968 Olympics.

"To even be in the same conversation with the likes of [them], is extremely humbling," he says. "But more importantly, I just try to stay focused on the work.

"What can we do to help people? And how do we collectively move forward as a society? And, ultimately, how we build a society that works for everybody. That feels like a very simple principle that has been lost.

"I know in the US specifically, we have a lot of work to do there. I hope we begin taking the steps to get back to a place where we are actually addressing people's needs. And create a society that is equitable for everyone."
authors: Dan Roan - Sports editor; Pat Nathanson - BBC Sport
